title: §.III: Historians of every party affirm that Luther sketched and Melanchthon finished what Augsburg presented
pass_a_gloss: §. III. Christians of whatever sect, and those skilled in the History of the Augsburg Confession, will acknowledge this description of the Augsburg Confession as true. For that it is a Complex of the chief Articles of the Christian Faith the Confession itself declares by its twenty-one Articles of its first Part, collated with Holy Scripture, the adequate principle of faith; and no less that this Complex is opposed chiefly to the papal party the same Confession most clearly sets out by the seven Heads of Abuses of its latter Part, if those Heads are compared with papal Confessions and Catechisms. But that that Complex was first sketched by Luther and more roughly conceived in seventeen Articles, and afterward more carefully worked out and more distinctly signed by Melanchthon — and even so approved by Luther equally and by some other theologians, Brenz, Jonas, Schnepf, Spalatin — and exhibited to the Emperor in the name of the said Estates at the place, time, and manner remembered (after it had been signed by their hands), exploded by him by public Decree, yet by them defended and confirmed, and indeed published the next year into public light in both the Latin and the German tongue in which it had been exhibited — all who have undertaken to adorn the History of the Augsburg Confession and to set out these matters of fact affirm with one mouth and with pens agreeing from every side, whose number, though not yet altogether full, Baclerus begins in the Memorial book of sixteenth-century affairs, pp. 405 and 406.
pass_b_english: §. III. Christians of every party, and anyone who knows the history of the Augsburg Confession, will own this description as true.
The Confession itself says it is a complex of the chief articles of Christian faith — through the twenty-one articles of its first part, set beside Holy Scripture, the adequate principle of faith.

No less clearly, through the seven heads of Abuses in its second part, it shows that this complex stands chiefly against the papal side, once those heads are compared with papal confessions and catechisms.

Luther first sketched that complex more roughly in seventeen articles; Melanchthon then worked it out more carefully and signed it more distinctly. Even in that shape Luther approved it, as did Brenz, Jonas, Schnepf, and Spalatin among other theologians.

In the name of those estates, at the place, time, and manner remembered — after their hands had signed it — it was shown to the Emperor, blasted by his public decree, yet defended and confirmed by them, and the next year published in both the Latin and the German in which it had been exhibited.

So say with one mouth, and with pens agreed from every side, all who have set out to write the Confession's history and narrate these facts — a company Baclerus begins to number, though the list is not yet full, in his Memorial of sixteenth-century affairs, pages 405–406.
source_text:
§. III.
Descriptionem hanc Augustanae Confessionis veram agnoverint cuicunque etiam Sectae addicti, Historiaeque Augustanae Confessionis gnari Christiani: Nam Articulorum Fidei Christianae praecipuorum Complexum, Augustanam Confessionem esse, ipsamet loquitur, per Articulos suos XXI. Partis suae prioris, cum Scriptura Sacra, fidei principio adaequato, collatos; idque non minus, ac Complexum hunc Pontificiis cumprimis oppositum esse, eadem, per Abusuum Partis suae posterioris Capita 7., clarissimè edisserit, si Capita haec cum Pontificiis Confessionibus & Catechismis comparentur. À Luthero verò Complexum illum delineatum primò, Articulisque XVII. rudius conceptum, ac postmodum à Melanchthone diligentius elaboratum distinctiùs consignatum, quanquam & sic quoque à Luthero pariter atque aliis nonnullis Theologis, Brentio, Jona, Snepfio, Spalatino approbatum, nomine Statuum dictorum, memoratis locô, tempore, modoque (postquam ab his subsignatus manibus esset) Caesari exhibitum, ab hoc publico Decreto explosum, ab istis tamen defensum, confirmatum, quin & in publicam lucem, lingvâ tàm Latinâ, quàm Germanicâ, in quibus exhibitus fuerat, Anno sequenti, editum esse, uno omnes ore & consentientibus undequaque calamis afferunt, quotquot Augustanae Confessionis Historiam adornare, resque has facti exponere aggressi sunt, quorum numerum, etsi nondum omnino plenum, Baclerus init, Lib. Memoriali de rebus Seculi XVI. p. m. 405. & 406.
